\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Motivation}
A walk in a graph is \emph{non-backtracking} if it never immediately reverses the edge it
has just traversed. The condition is small and decisive. Ordinary walks on sparse graphs
waste a constant fraction of their steps undoing the previous one; their closed-walk counts
are swamped by trivial there-and-back contributions, and their spectral theory is dominated
by degree fluctuations. Removing backtracking removes exactly this noise, leaving an object
whose closed orbits are, in a precise sense, the \emph{cycles} of the graph. Three separate
areas depend on this.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Zeta functions.} Ihara's zeta function of a graph is an Euler product over
equivalence classes of primitive closed non-backtracking cycles, and its expression as a
finite determinant rests on interpreting $\tr(B^{n})$ as a count of such walks.
\item \textbf{Spectral inference.} In sparse random graph models the leading eigenvectors
of the adjacency matrix localise on high-degree vertices; those of the non-backtracking
matrix do not, and non-backtracking spectral methods achieve community detection down to
the information-theoretic threshold for the stochastic block model.
\item \textbf{Expansion.} For $(q+1)$-regular graphs, the Ramanujan property is equivalent
to the nontrivial spectrum of $B$ lying on the circle of radius $\sqrt{q}$, the square root
of the non-backtracking branching factor.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{The obstacle: asymmetry}
For a simple graph with adjacency matrix $A$, the identity
$(A^{n})_{uv}=\#\{\text{walks of length }n\text{ from }u\text{ to }v\}$ is standard, and it
is standardly proved using the symmetric structure of the graph. The non-backtracking
successor relation lives on \emph{darts}, and it is not symmetric; indeed it is
antisymmetric in the strongest sense (Lemma~\ref{lem:asym}): if $e$ may follow $d$ then $d$
may never follow $e$. The correct level of generality is a decidable binary relation on a
finite index set, i.e.\ an arbitrary digraph, and Section~\ref{sec:rel} develops walk
counting there before Section~\ref{sec:main} specialises.

\section{Walk counting for an arbitrary finite relation}\label{sec:rel}

Throughout this section $\iota$ is a finite set with decidable equality and
$r\subseteq\iota\times\iota$ is a binary relation --- equivalently a digraph on $\iota$,
possibly with loops and certainly not assumed symmetric.

\begin{definition}[Relation matrix]
The \emph{relation matrix} of $r$ is $M=M(r)\in\mathbb{N}^{\iota\times\iota}$ with
$M_{ij}=1$ if $r(i,j)$ and $M_{ij}=0$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Walks]
For $n\ge 0$ and $a,b\in\iota$, a \emph{walk of length $n$ from $a$ to $b$} is a list
$\ell=(\ell_{0},\dots,\ell_{n})$ of $n+1$ elements of $\iota$ with $\ell_{0}=a$,
$\ell_{n}=b$ and $r(\ell_{i},\ell_{i+1})$ for $0\le i<n$. Write $W_{n}(a,b)$ for the set of
such walks.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Rooted closed walks]
A \emph{rooted closed walk of length $n$} is a walk of length $n$ from $a$ to $a$ for some
$a$; set $C_{n}=\bigsqcup_{a\in\iota}W_{n}(a,a)$. The adjective \emph{rooted} records that
the starting point is part of the data: the same cyclic pattern started at a different
index is a different element of $C_{n}$. Note $|C_{0}|=|\iota|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Entries of powers count walks]\label{thm:entries}
For all $n\ge 0$ and $a,b\in\iota$ we have $(M^{n})_{ab}=|W_{n}(a,b)|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $n$. For $n=0$, $M^{0}=I$ and $W_{0}(a,b)$ is a singleton when $a=b$ and empty
otherwise. For the step, expand $(M^{n+1})_{ab}=\sum_{c}M_{ac}(M^{n})_{cb}$. Each summand
equals $|W_{n}(c,b)|$ when $r(a,c)$ and vanishes otherwise, and
$\ell\mapsto (a)\mathbin{+\!\!+}\ell$ is a bijection from
$\bigsqcup_{c:\,r(a,c)}W_{n}(c,b)$ onto $W_{n+1}(a,b)$: prepending $a$ to a chain from $c$
to $b$ produces a chain from $a$ exactly when $r(a,c)$, and every walk of length $n+1$
starting at $a$ arises uniquely by stripping its head.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Trace counts rooted closed walks]\label{thm:trace-general}
For all $n\ge 0$, $\tr(M^{n})=|C_{n}|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\tr(M^{n})=\sum_{a}(M^{n})_{aa}=\sum_{a}|W_{n}(a,a)|=|C_{n}|$, the union being disjoint
since the sets $W_{n}(a,a)$ are distinguished by their first entry.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Constant row sums]\label{prop:rowsum-general}
If $\sum_{j}M_{ij}=q$ for all $i$, then every row of $M^{n}$ sums to $q^{n}$, and
consequently $\tr(M^{n})\le\sum_{i,j}(M^{n})_{ij}=|\iota|\,q^{n}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$M\mathbf{1}=q\mathbf{1}$ gives $M^{n}\mathbf{1}=q^{n}\mathbf{1}$ by induction; all entries
are nonnegative and the trace is a partial sum of all entries.
\end{proof}

\section{Darts, non-backtracking succession, and the main theorem}\label{sec:main}

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph, and write $u\sim v$ for adjacency.

\subsection{Darts}
\begin{definition}[Dart]
A \emph{dart} of $G$ is an ordered pair $d=(u,v)$ with $u\sim v$. Write
$\degtail(d)=u$, $\deghead(d)=v$ and $d^{-1}=(v,u)$ for the \emph{reversal}, and let
$\Darts(G)$ be the set of darts, so that
$|\Darts(G)|=2|E|=\sum_{v\in V}\deg(v)$. The \emph{underlying edge} of $d=(u,v)$ is
$\{u,v\}$.
\end{definition}

Since $G$ is loopless, $d\neq d^{-1}$ for every dart: reversal is a fixed-point-free
involution of $\Darts(G)$. This remark is the entire content of Theorem~\ref{thm:even}.

\subsection{The non-backtracking relation}
\begin{definition}[Non-backtracking succession]\label{def:nb}
For darts $d=(u,v)$ and $e=(x,y)$, say that \emph{$e$ may follow $d$}, written
$d\to e$, if $v=x$ and $y\neq u$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Reformulation]
$d\to e$ if and only if $\deghead(d)=\degtail(e)$ and $e\neq d^{-1}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Given $\deghead(d)=\degtail(e)$, the darts $e$ and $d^{-1}$ share their tail, so $e=d^{-1}$
iff their heads agree, i.e.\ $y=u$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Irreflexivity and strong asymmetry]\label{lem:asym}
For all darts $d,e$: (i) $d\not\to d$; (ii) if $d\to e$ then $e\not\to d$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) $d\to d$ would force $v=u$, impossible in a loopless graph. (ii) If $d=(u,v)\to e=(x,y)$
then $v=x$ and $y\neq u$; if also $e\to d$ then $y=u$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Hashimoto matrix]
The \emph{Hashimoto matrix} of $G$ is the relation matrix
$B=M(\to)\in\mathbb{N}^{\Darts(G)\times\Darts(G)}$, a square matrix of size $2|E|$ with
zero diagonal satisfying $B\circ B^{\T}=0$ entrywise, by Lemma~\ref{lem:asym}.
\end{definition}

\subsection{The counting theorem}

\begin{definition}
A \emph{rooted closed non-backtracking walk of length $n$} in $G$ is a list of darts
$(d_{0},\dots,d_{n})$ with $d_{i}\to d_{i+1}$ for $0\le i<n$ and $d_{n}=d_{0}$. Write
$\Cwalks_{n}(G)$ for the set of these.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Non-Backtracking Trace Formula]\label{thm:main}
For every finite simple graph $G$ and every $n\ge 0$,
\[
  \tr(B^{n})\;=\;|\Cwalks_{n}(G)|.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:trace-general} to the finite index set $\Darts(G)$ and the relation
$\to$.
\end{proof}

The economy of this proof is due entirely to having set up Section~\ref{sec:rel} at the
right level of generality; the combinatorial substance lives there.

\subsection{The cyclic-word form}

\begin{definition}[Cyclic non-backtracking words]
For $n\ge 1$, let $\Zwords_{n}(G)$ be the set of lists $c=(c_{1},\dots,c_{n})$ of darts
with $c_{i}\to c_{i+1}$ for $1\le i<n$ (the \emph{chain condition}) and $c_{n}\to c_{1}$
(the \emph{seam condition}). Writing $\sigma$ for the cyclic shift, this is the single
pointwise condition $c_{i}\to(\sigma c)_{i}$ for all $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:cyclic}
For $n\ge 1$, deletion of the last entry is a bijection
$\Cwalks_{n}(G)\to\Zwords_{n}(G)$; hence $\tr(B^{n})=|\Zwords_{n}(G)|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Deletion preserves the chain condition, and the seam condition is the link
$d_{n-1}\to d_{n}=d_{0}$ rewritten. It is injective because the deleted entry is recoverable
as the first entry, and surjective because appending $c_{1}$ to $c\in\Zwords_{n}(G)$
restores a closed walk, the seam condition supplying the final link. Now apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Stability of cyclic words]\label{prop:stability}
For $n\ge 1$, the set $\Zwords_{n}(G)$ is stable under (i) rotation $c\mapsto\sigma^{i}c$
for every $i$, and (ii) the reversal
$c\mapsto\overline{c}:=(c_{n}^{-1},c_{n-1}^{-1},\dots,c_{1}^{-1})$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(i) The pointwise formulation is preserved by applying $\sigma^{i}$ to both sides, since
$\sigma^{i}$ commutes with $\sigma$. (ii) Definition~\ref{def:nb} gives
$d\to e\iff e^{-1}\to d^{-1}$; reversing the list therefore converts the chain condition
into itself with endpoints exchanged, and likewise for the seam.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The vertex form}

\begin{theorem}[Vertex form]\label{thm:vertex}
For $n\ge 1$,
\[
  \tr(B^{n})=\#\bigl\{(u_{1},\dots,u_{n})\in V^{n}\;:\;u_{i}\sim u_{i+1}\ \text{and}\
  u_{i+2}\neq u_{i}\ \text{for all }i\ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)\bigr\}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Map $c\in\Zwords_{n}(G)$ to its sequence of tails $u_{i}=\degtail(c_{i})$. Since
$c_{i}\to c_{i+1}$ forces $\deghead(c_{i})=u_{i+1}$, we have $c_{i}=(u_{i},u_{i+1})$, so the
map is injective. Adjacency holds because $c_{i}$ is a dart, and the non-backtracking clause
of $c_{i}\to c_{i+1}$ reads $\deghead(c_{i+1})\neq\degtail(c_{i})$, i.e.\
$u_{i+2}\neq u_{i}$. Conversely such a vertex sequence lifts by $c_{i}:=(u_{i},u_{i+1})$.
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:cyclic}.
\end{proof}

The vertex form makes the constraint transparent: a closed non-backtracking walk is an
ordinary closed walk avoiding a single \emph{local forbidden pattern}, namely
$u_{i+2}=u_{i}$ at distance two.

\section{Small powers, row sums and growth}

\begin{proposition}
$\tr(B^{0})=|\Darts(G)|=2|E|=\sum_{v\in V}\deg(v)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:tr1}
$\tr(B)=0$ for every graph.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The diagonal entries $B_{d,d}$ vanish by Lemma~\ref{lem:asym}(i).
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:tr2}
$\tr(B^{2})=0$ for every graph.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$(B^{2})_{d,d}=\sum_{f}B_{d,f}B_{f,d}$, and each product vanishes by
Lemma~\ref{lem:asym}(ii).
\end{proof}

Equivalently, no graph has a rooted closed non-backtracking walk of length $1$ or $2$.
Contrast $\tr(A^{2})=2|E|$ for the adjacency matrix: the entire length-two closed-walk
count of a graph consists of backtracks.

\begin{definition}
An \emph{ordered triangle} of $G$ is a triple $(a,b,c)\in V^{3}$ with $a\sim b$, $b\sim c$,
$c\sim a$. The three adjacencies force $a,b,c$ pairwise distinct, so the ordered triangles
are the $6$ orderings of each triangle.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:triangles}
$\tr(B^{3})=\#\{\text{ordered triangles of }G\}=6\cdot\#\{\text{triangles of }G\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:cyclic} we count cyclic words of three darts. An ordered triangle
$(a,b,c)$ gives the word $((a,b),(b,c),(c,a))$, whose chain and seam conditions read
$c\neq a$, $a\neq b$, $b\neq c$: all true. The assignment is injective, the triangle being
read off from the tails, and surjective by Theorem~\ref{thm:vertex}: a cyclic vertex
sequence of length three with the two constraints is exactly an ordered triangle.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Row-sum identity]\label{thm:rowsum}
For every dart $d$, $\displaystyle\sum_{e\in \Darts(G)}B_{d,e}=\deg(\deghead(d))-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $d=(u,v)$. The darts $e$ with $d\to e$ are exactly the darts with tail $v$ other than
$(v,u)$. There are $\deg(v)$ darts with tail $v$, one per neighbour, and exactly one is
excluded.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
If $G$ is $(q+1)$-regular then every row of $B$ sums to $q$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Growth bound]\label{thm:growth}
If $G$ is $(q+1)$-regular then $\tr(B^{n})\le 2|E|\,q^{n}$ for all $n\ge 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine the corollary with Proposition~\ref{prop:rowsum-general}, taking
$|\iota|=|\Darts(G)|=2|E|$.
\end{proof}

The exponential rate is $q$, not $q+1$: at each step the walker forfeits one of its $q+1$
options. The associated spectral scale $\sqrt{q}$ is the Alon--Boppana/Ramanujan threshold.

\section{Parity: the reversal involution}

\begin{definition}
For a list of darts $\ell=(d_{0},\dots,d_{n})$, set
$\overline{\ell}:=(d_{n}^{-1},d_{n-1}^{-1},\dots,d_{0}^{-1})$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:rev}
$\overline{\overline{\ell}}=\ell$, and if $\ell\in\Cwalks_{n}(G)$ then
$\overline{\ell}\in\Cwalks_{n}(G)$ and $\overline{\ell}\neq\ell$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Involutivity is immediate. Stability: $d\to e\iff e^{-1}\to d^{-1}$ by
Definition~\ref{def:nb}, so the chain condition survives reversal; the length is unchanged;
and $d_{n}=d_{0}$ becomes $d_{0}^{-1}=d_{n}^{-1}$. Fixed-point-freeness: if
$\overline{\ell}=\ell$, comparing first entries gives $d_{0}=d_{n}^{-1}=d_{0}^{-1}$,
contradicting $d\neq d^{-1}$ in a loopless graph.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Evenness]\label{thm:even}
For every finite simple graph $G$ and every $n\ge 0$, the integer $\tr(B^{n})$ is even.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:main} it suffices that $|\Cwalks_{n}(G)|$ be even. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:rev}, $\ell\mapsto\overline{\ell}$ is a fixed-point-free involution of a
finite set, so all its orbits have size $2$ and they partition the set into pairs.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Reversal intertwines $B$ with its transpose]\label{thm:JBJ}
Let $J$ be the permutation matrix of $d\mapsto d^{-1}$, so $J=J^{-1}$. Then
\[
  J\,B\,J = B^{\T},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad B_{d^{-1},e^{-1}}=B_{e,d}\quad\text{for
  all darts }d,e .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The entry identity is precisely $e^{-1}\to d^{-1}\iff d\to e$, and conjugation by the
permutation matrix $J$ is the corresponding simultaneous relabelling of rows and columns.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:JBJ} says that $B$ is similar to $B^{\T}$ by an \emph{explicit
involution}, not merely by the abstract similarity valid for every square matrix. It is the
structural reason behind the evenness of the traces and behind the symmetry of the
non-backtracking spectrum.

\section{Acyclicity}

\begin{theorem}[Cycles force a positive trace]\label{thm:cycpos}
If $G$ contains a cycle of length $m$, i.e.\ a closed walk of length $m\ge 3$ with pairwise
distinct, cyclically adjacent vertices $u_{1},\dots,u_{m}$, then $\tr(B^{m})\ge 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:vertex} it suffices to exhibit one admissible cyclic vertex sequence of
length $m$; take $(u_{1},\dots,u_{m})$. Adjacency holds by hypothesis, and $u_{i+2}\neq
u_{i}$ holds because the $u_{j}$ are pairwise distinct and $m\ge 3$ ensures
$i+2\not\equiv i \pmod m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Forests have vanishing traces]\label{thm:forest}
If $G$ contains no cycle then $\tr(B^{n})=0$ for every $n\ge 1$; equivalently
$\Cwalks_{n}(G)=\emptyset$ for $n\ge 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Suppose $c\in\Zwords_{n}(G)$ with $n\ge 1$.

\emph{Step 1: darts reassemble into a walk.} A list of darts with
$\deghead(c_{i})=\degtail(c_{i+1})$ is the dart list of a genuine walk in $G$ from
$\degtail(c_{1})$ to $\deghead(c_{n})$, by induction on the list, prepending one edge at a
time. The seam condition gives $\deghead(c_{n})=\degtail(c_{1})$, so the walk $p$ is closed,
of length $n\ge 1$.

\emph{Step 2: consecutive edges differ.} If $d\to e$ then the underlying edges of $d$ and
$e$ differ: equality of $\{u,v\}$ and $\{v,y\}$ forces $u=v$ (excluded: no loops) or $y=u$
(excluded: the non-backtracking clause). So the edge list of $p$ has distinct consecutive
entries.

In a forest a walk with distinct consecutive edges is a path, hence has no repeated vertex;
a closed path has length $0$, contradicting $n\ge 1$. Thus $\Zwords_{n}(G)=\emptyset$, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:cyclic} concludes.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Acyclicity criterion]\label{thm:acyc}
For a finite simple graph $G$,
\[
  G\ \text{is a forest}\iff \tr(B^{n})=0\ \text{for all }n\ge 1 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) is Theorem~\ref{thm:forest}. ($\Leftarrow$) contrapositively: a cycle of
length $m$ gives $\tr(B^{m})\ge 1$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:cycpos}, and $m\ge 3\ge 1$.
\end{proof}

\section{Girth}

Let $g(G)$ denote the girth, the least length of a cycle, with $g(G)=\infty$ for forests.

\begin{theorem}[No trace below the girth]\label{thm:girthupper}
If $n\ge 1$ and $\tr(B^{n})\neq 0$, then $g(G)\le n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:cyclic} there is $c\in\Zwords_{n}(G)$, and Steps 1--2 of the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:forest} produce a closed walk $p$ of length $n\ge 1$ with distinct
consecutive edges. Let $H\subseteq G$ be spanned by the edges of $p$. Then $H$ is not
acyclic, since otherwise $p$, living in $H$ with distinct consecutive edges, would be a path
and hence of length $0$. So $H$ contains a cycle of length at most $|E(H)|\le n$, and
$H\subseteq G$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
If $1\le n<g(G)$ then $\tr(B^{n})=0$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Girth criterion]\label{thm:girth}
If $G$ contains a cycle then
$\displaystyle g(G)=\min\{\,n\ge 1: \tr(B^{n})\neq 0\,\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A shortest cycle has length $g(G)\ge 3$ and gives $\tr(B^{g(G)})\ge 1$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:cycpos}, so $g(G)$ lies in the set; every element $n$ of the set satisfies
$n\ge g(G)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:girthupper}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Multiplicity at the girth]\label{thm:mult}
If $p$ is a cycle of length $m$ in $G$, then $2m\le\tr(B^{m})$. In particular, if $G$
contains a cycle then $2\,g(G)\le\tr\bigl(B^{\,g(G)}\bigr)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $c\in\Zwords_{m}(G)$ be the dart word of $p$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:stability} the
$2m$ words $\sigma^{i}c$ and $\sigma^{i}\overline{c}$, $0\le i<m$, all lie in
$\Zwords_{m}(G)$, and they are pairwise distinct: the $m$ rotations of $c$ are distinct
because $c$ has pairwise distinct entries (its darts have distinct tails, the vertices of
the cycle), similarly for $\overline{c}$; and no rotation of $c$ equals one of
$\overline{c}$, since the entries of $c$ traverse the cycle in one orientation and those of
$\overline{c}$ in the other, giving disjoint entry sets. Hence
$|\Zwords_{m}(G)|\ge 2m$.
\end{proof}

The bound is sharp: for the cycle graph $C_{m}$ one has $\tr(B^{m})=2m$ exactly. When
several shortest cycles exist the bound is strict, and the data suggest
$\tr(B^{g})=2g\cdot\#\{\text{cycles of length }g\}$ (Problem~\ref{prob:mult}).

\section{Monotonicity under subgraph inclusion}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:mono}
Let $H\subseteq G$ be graphs on the same vertex set, with Hashimoto matrices $B_{H}$ and
$B_{G}$. Then $\tr(B_{H}^{\,n})\le\tr(B_{G}^{\,n})$ for every $n\ge 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $n=0$ both sides are dart counts and $|\Darts(H)|\le|\Darts(G)|$. For $n\ge 1$ the
inclusion $\Darts(H)\hookrightarrow\Darts(G)$ is injective and both preserves and reflects
the non-backtracking relation, because that relation refers only to the endpoints of the
darts and not to the ambient edge set. Applying it entrywise maps $\Zwords_{n}(H)$
injectively into $\Zwords_{n}(G)$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:cyclic} converts the resulting
inequality of cardinalities into the stated inequality of traces.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The proof is combinatorial by necessity: $B_{H}$ and $B_{G}$ do not even have the same size,
and entrywise domination of non-symmetric matrices does not in general survive taking
powers.
\end{remark}

\section{Worked examples}

\subsection{The triangle $K_{3}$}
$K_{3}$ has $3$ edges and $6$ darts, and by Theorem~\ref{thm:rowsum} every row of $B$ sums
to $\deg-1=1$: each dart has a unique legal continuation. Thus $B$ is a permutation matrix,
a product of two $3$-cycles (one per orientation), so
\[
  B^{3}=I_{6},\qquad
  \tr(B^{n})=\begin{cases}6,&3\mid n,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]
For $n=3k+1$ and $n=3k+2$ the trace reduces to $\tr(B)$ and $\tr(B^{2})$, both zero by
Propositions~\ref{prop:tr1} and \ref{prop:tr2}. The value $6=2\cdot 3$ realises
Theorem~\ref{thm:mult} with equality.

\subsection{The complete graph $K_{4}$}
$K_{4}$ has $6$ edges, $12$ darts, four triangles and three quadrilaterals.
Theorem~\ref{thm:triangles} gives $\tr(B^{3})=6\cdot 4=24$, and direct evaluation gives
$\tr(B^{4})=24=8\cdot 3$, each quadrilateral contributing $2\cdot 4=8$ words. Being
$3$-regular, $K_{4}$ has $q=2$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:growth} predicts
$\tr(B^{n})\le 12\cdot 2^{n}$; at $n=3$ this reads $24\le 96$.

\subsection{The pentagon $C_{5}$}
$C_{5}$ has $10$ darts and again a unique continuation per dart, so $B$ is a permutation of
order $5$:
\[
  B^{5}=I_{10},\qquad
  \tr(B^{n})=\begin{cases}10,&5\mid n,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise }(n\ge 1).\end{cases}
\]
The first nonvanishing index is $5=g(C_{5})$, confirming Theorem~\ref{thm:girth}, and
$10=2\cdot 5$ meets Theorem~\ref{thm:mult} with equality. In general $C_{m}$ has
$\tr(B^{n})=2m$ when $m\mid n$ and $0$ otherwise.

\subsection{A tree}
For the path $P_{3}: 0-1-2$ (four darts) one computes $B^{2}=0$: the Hashimoto matrix of a
tree is nilpotent, so all traces of positive powers vanish, illustrating
Theorem~\ref{thm:forest}.

\subsection{The Petersen graph}
Cubic, $15$ edges, $30$ darts, girth $5$, with exactly $12$ pentagons. The trace sequence
begins $30,0,0,0,0,120,120$ for $n=0,\dots,6$. The first nonzero index is $5$, as
Theorem~\ref{thm:girth} requires, and $120=2\cdot 5\cdot 12$: each shortest cycle counted
with multiplicity $2\cdot 5$. The growth bound with $q=2$ gives $\tr(B^{5})\le 30\cdot 32
=960$.

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Building the matrix}
Enumerating darts and testing Definition~\ref{def:nb} pairwise builds $B$ in
$O((2|E|)^{2})$ time and space. In sparse form the row of $(u,v)$ has $\deg(v)-1$ nonzeros,
so $B$ has $\sum_{v}\deg(v)^{2}-2|E|$ nonzeros; for a $(q+1)$-regular graph this is
$2|E|q$.

\subsection{Trace of a power}
Two regimes. Dense, single $n$: repeated squaring computes $B^{n}$ in
$O(\log n\cdot(2|E|)^{\omega})$ arithmetic operations, with entries of size $O(q^{n})$, so
exact-integer bit complexity carries an extra factor $O(n\log q)$. Sparse, all $n\le N$:
compute $\tr(B^{n})$ as $\sum_{d}(B^{n})_{dd}$ by running $2|E|$ sparse matrix--vector
products of length $n$, giving $O(N\cdot\mathrm{nnz}(B)\cdot 2|E|)$ for the whole prefix.

\subsection{Girth by trace search}
Theorem~\ref{thm:girth} yields an algorithm: evaluate $\tr(B),\tr(B^{2}),\dots$ and return
the first index with a nonzero value, reporting ``forest'' if the search passes $|V|$.
Correctness is Theorem~\ref{thm:girth} together with Theorem~\ref{thm:acyc}. This is
inferior to breadth-first search as a practical girth algorithm, but instructive as a
\emph{certificate}: a nonzero trace at index $n$ certifies $g\le n$, and vanishing traces up
to $n$ certify $g>n$.

\subsection{Verifying the counting theorem}
Enumerate all rooted closed non-backtracking walks of length $n$ by depth-first search from
each dart, following only legal successors and accepting a path of $n+1$ darts that returns
to its root. The enumeration costs $O(2|E|\,q^{n})$ in the regular case --- precisely the
bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:growth}.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{The Ihara zeta function}
For a finite graph the Ihara zeta function is
$\zeta_{G}(u)=\prod_{[\gamma]}(1-u^{\ell(\gamma)})^{-1}$, the product over rotation classes
of primitive closed non-backtracking cycles. Taking logarithmic derivatives converts the
product into a sum over all closed non-backtracking walks, which Theorem~\ref{thm:main}
identifies with $\sum_{n\ge 1}\tr(B^{n})u^{n}$. The consequent identity
\[
  \sum_{n\ge 1}\frac{\tr(B^{n})}{n}u^{n}=-\log\det(I-uB),\qquad \zeta_{G}(u)=\det(I-uB)^{-1},
\]
reduces an infinite Euler product to a finite determinant, and Ihara's theorem collapses
that determinant further for $(q+1)$-regular graphs:
\[
  \det(I-uB)=(1-u^{2})^{|E|-|V|}\det\!\left(I-uA+qu^{2}I\right).
\]

\subsection{Non-backtracking spectra in inference}
The eigenvalues of $B$ govern the mixing of the non-backtracking random walk. In sparse
random graphs with heavy-tailed degrees, the adjacency matrix's leading eigenvectors
localise on hubs; the Hashimoto matrix suppresses this, since a walker unable to U-turn
cannot dwell on a hub by oscillating across one edge. Non-backtracking spectral methods
consequently detect planted community structure in the sparse stochastic block model down to
the Kesten--Stigum threshold, where adjacency-based methods fail.

\subsection{What the trace sequence sees}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Feature of the sequence & Meaning for the graph\\
\midrule
$\tr(B^{0})=2|E|$ & number of darts\\
$\tr(B^{1})=\tr(B^{2})=0$ & holds universally\\
$\tr(B^{3})$ & $6\times$ number of triangles\\
all terms even & dart reversal pairs walks; $JBJ=B^{\T}$\\
identically zero & $G$ is a forest\\
index of first nonzero term & the girth $g(G)$\\
value there, $\ge 2g$ & shortest cycles counted $2g$ times each\\
nondecreasing under $H\subseteq G$ & monotone in the edge set\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The sequence is insensitive to pendant trees: any tree part contributes nothing to a
positive power, so the non-backtracking trace sequence is an invariant of the $2$-core, and
two graphs with the same $2$-core have identical sequences except at $n=0$.

\subsection{On the necessity of darts}
The vertex form might suggest that darts are dispensable. They are not, for the counting
theorem itself: the constraint $u_{i+2}\neq u_{i}$ is not a condition on consecutive terms
of the vertex sequence, and is therefore not encoded by any matrix indexed by vertices.
Passing to darts makes the constraint local, and locality is exactly what a matrix
expresses. The price is a state space of size $2|E|$ instead of $|V|$.

\section{Open problems}

\begin{problem}[Chebyshev-like recursion]
For a $(q+1)$-regular graph with adjacency matrix $A$, let $A_{m}$ count non-backtracking
walks of length $m$ between vertices.
\begin{conjecture}
$A_{1}=A$, $A_{2}=A^{2}-(q+1)I$, and $A_{m+1}=A\,A_{m}-q\,A_{m-1}$ for $m\ge 2$;
consequently $A_{m}=P_{m}(A)$ for an explicit Chebyshev-like polynomial $P_{m}$, and
$\tr(B^{m})$ is a fixed linear combination of the numbers $\tr(A^{k})$, $k\le m$.
\end{conjecture}
The vertex form (Theorem~\ref{thm:vertex}) exhibits closed non-backtracking walks as
ordinary walks with a single forbidden local pattern, so inclusion--exclusion on that
pattern should close into a three-term recursion; the coefficient $q$ is the row sum of
Theorem~\ref{thm:rowsum}.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Ihara identity from the trace generating function]
\begin{conjecture}
$\sum_{n\ge 1}\tr(B^{n})u^{n}/n=-\log\det(I-uB)$ for every finite graph, and for
$(q+1)$-regular graphs the right-hand side equals
$-\log[(1-u^{2})^{|E|-|V|}\det(I-uA+qu^{2}I)]$.
\end{conjecture}
The counting theorem converts the analytic identity into a statement about cyclic words, so
the hard direction becomes a bijection between cyclic non-backtracking words and multisets
of primitive cycles. Proposition~\ref{prop:stability} supplies the rotation and reversal
stability needed for the primitive-cycle decomposition; what remains is orbit--stabiliser
bookkeeping.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Exact multiplicity at the girth]\label{prob:mult}
\begin{conjecture}
For a graph containing a cycle, with $g=g(G)$,
\[
  \tr(B^{\,g})=2g\cdot\#\{\text{cycles of length }g\},
\]
so the first nonzero term of the trace sequence counts shortest cycles with multiplicity
exactly $2g$.
\end{conjecture}
Theorem~\ref{thm:mult} supplies the inequality $\ge 2g$; the converse requires that every
cyclic non-backtracking word of length exactly $g$ be the dart word of a cycle, which
minimality of $g$ should force. The identity is confirmed on $C_{5}$ ($10$), $K_{4}$ ($24$),
$K_{3,3}$ ($72$) and the Petersen graph ($120$).
\end{problem}

\section{Conclusion}

The non-backtracking trace formula
$\tr(B^{n})=\#\{\text{rooted closed non-backtracking walks of length }n\}$ is elementary,
but it is a hinge. On one side lies linear algebra: powers, traces, eigenvalues,
determinants. On the other lies the cycle structure of a graph: triangles, girth,
acyclicity, multiplicity. The proof requires walk counting for a general directed relation,
because non-backtracking succession is asymmetric by nature; once that groundwork is laid,
the theorem is a two-line consequence. What follows from it is not: the acyclicity
criterion, the girth criterion, the multiplicity bound at the girth, the parity of every
trace with its source in dart reversal, and the monotonicity of the whole sequence under
adding edges are each substantive statements about graphs, each most naturally proved by
passing through the walk interpretation.

The general lesson: a global constraint that is not a function of the current state can
often be made local by enlarging the state. Darts are the enlargement that makes
non-backtracking local; a matrix is what locality buys; and everything above is what the
matrix pays out.

For a finite simple graph G = (V, E) let

    D = { (u, v) : {u, v} in E }

be its set of *darts* (each undirected edge gives two darts, so |D| = 2|E|).
The Hashimoto (non-backtracking) matrix B is the |D| x |D| zero-one matrix

    B[(u,v), (x,y)] = 1   iff   v = x  and  y != u.

A *rooted closed non-backtracking walk of length n* is a list of n + 1 darts
d_0, d_1, ..., d_n with B[d_i, d_{i+1}] = 1 for all i and d_0 = d_n.

Main theorem demonstrated here:

    trace(B^n) = # { rooted closed non-backtracking walks of length n }.

Together with its corollaries:

  * trace(B^0) = |D| = sum of degrees,  trace(B^1) = trace(B^2) = 0;
  * trace(B^3) = number of ordered triangles (= 6 * #triangles);
  * every trace(B^n) is even (dart reversal is a fixed-point-free involution);
  * row sums: sum_{d'} B[d, d'] = deg(head(d)) - 1; for a (q+1)-regular graph
    every row sums to q, so trace(B^n) <= |D| * q^n;
  * G is a forest  iff  trace(B^n) = 0 for all n >= 1;
  * girth(G) = min { n >= 1 : trace(B^n) != 0 }, and 2 * girth(G) <= trace(B^girth);
  * H subgraph of G  implies  trace(B_H^n) <= trace(B_G^n).

Everything below is plain Python with no third-party dependencies: the matrix
powers are computed with exact integer arithmetic, and the walk counts are
obtained by explicit enumeration, so the two sides of the theorem are compared
by two genuinely independent computations.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Vertex = int
Edge = FrozenSet[Vertex]
Dart = Tuple[Vertex, Vertex]
Matrix = List[List[int]]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Graphs
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

class Graph:
    """A finite simple graph on the vertex set {0, ..., n-1}."""

    def __init__(self, n: int, edges: Iterable[Tuple[Vertex, Vertex]]) -> None:
        self.n: int = n
        self.edges: List[Edge] = []
        seen: Set[Edge] = set()
        for u, v in edges:
            if u == v:
                raise ValueError("simple graphs have no loops")
            e = frozenset((u, v))
            if e not in seen:
                seen.add(e)
                self.edges.append(e)
        self.adj: Dict[Vertex, Set[Vertex]] = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
        for e in self.edges:
            u, v = tuple(e)
            self.adj[u].add(v)
            self.adj[v].add(u)

    def degree(self, v: Vertex) -> int:
        return len(self.adj[v])

    def darts(self) -> List[Dart]:
        """All darts, in a fixed deterministic order."""
        out: List[Dart] = []
        for e in sorted(self.edges, key=lambda s: sorted(s)):
            u, v = sorted(e)
            out.append((u, v))
            out.append((v, u))
        return out

    def is_regular(self) -> Optional[int]:
        """Return the common degree if the graph is regular, else None."""
        degs = {self.degree(v) for v in range(self.n)}
        return degs.pop() if len(degs) == 1 else None


def complete_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    return Graph(n, combinations(range(n), 2))


def cycle_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    return Graph(n, [(i, (i + 1) % n) for i in range(n)])


def path_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    return Graph(n, [(i, i + 1) for i in range(n - 1)])


def petersen_graph() -> Graph:
    outer = [(i, (i + 1) % 5) for i in range(5)]
    inner = [(5 + i, 5 + (i + 2) % 5) for i in range(5)]
    spokes = [(i, 5 + i) for i in range(5)]
    return Graph(10, outer + inner + spokes)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The Hashimoto matrix and exact integer linear algebra
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def nb_adjacent(d: Dart, e: Dart) -> bool:
    """Non-backtracking succession: d = (u,v) is followed by e = (x,y)."""
    (u, v), (x, y) = d, e
    return v == x and y != u


def hashimoto(g: Graph) -> Matrix:
    darts = g.darts()
    return [[1 if nb_adjacent(d, e) else 0 for e in darts] for d in darts]


def mat_mul(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    n, m, p = len(a), len(b), len(b[0])
    out = [[0] * p for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n):
        row = a[i]
        oi = out[i]
        for k in range(m):
            aik = row[k]
            if aik:
                bk = b[k]
                for j in range(p):
                    oi[j] += aik * bk[j]
    return out


def mat_identity(n: int) -> Matrix:
    return [[1 if i == j else 0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def mat_pow(a: Matrix, n: int) -> Matrix:
    """Exact integer matrix power by repeated squaring."""
    result = mat_identity(len(a))
    base = [row[:] for row in a]
    while n:
        if n & 1:
            result = mat_mul(result, base)
        base = mat_mul(base, base)
        n >>= 1
    return result


def trace(a: Matrix) -> int:
    return sum(a[i][i] for i in range(len(a)))


def nb_trace(g: Graph, n: int) -> int:
    return trace(mat_pow(hashimoto(g), n))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Brute-force enumeration of rooted closed non-backtracking walks
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def closed_nb_walks(g: Graph, n: int) -> List[Tuple[Dart, ...]]:
    """All rooted closed non-backtracking walks of length n, as dart lists."""
    darts = g.darts()
    if n == 0:
        return [(d,) for d in darts]
    successors: Dict[Dart, List[Dart]] = {
        d: [e for e in darts if nb_adjacent(d, e)] for d in darts
    }
    out: List[Tuple[Dart, ...]] = []

    def extend(prefix: List[Dart]) -> None:
        if len(prefix) == n + 1:
            if prefix[0] == prefix[-1]:
                out.append(tuple(prefix))
            return
        for e in successors[prefix[-1]]:
            prefix.append(e)
            extend(prefix)
            prefix.pop()

    for d in darts:
        extend([d])
    return out


def count_closed_nb_walks(g: Graph, n: int) -> int:
    return len(closed_nb_walks(g, n))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Combinatorial invariants used by the corollaries
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def ordered_triangles(g: Graph) -> int:
    """Number of triples (a,b,c) with a~b, b~c, c~a; equals 6 * #triangles."""
    return sum(
        1
        for a in range(g.n)
        for b in g.adj[a]
        for c in g.adj[b]
        if a in g.adj[c]
    )


def girth(g: Graph) -> Optional[int]:
    """Length of a shortest cycle, or None for a forest (BFS from each vertex)."""
    best: Optional[int] = None
    for root in range(g.n):
        dist = {root: 0}
        parent: Dict[Vertex, Optional[Vertex]] = {root: None}
        queue = [root]
        while queue:
            nxt: List[Vertex] = []
            for u in queue:
                for w in g.adj[u]:
                    if w not in dist:
                        dist[w] = dist[u] + 1
                        parent[w] = u
                        nxt.append(w)
                    elif parent[u] != w:
                        cand = dist[u] + dist[w] + 1
                        best = cand if best is None else min(best, cand)
            queue = nxt
    return best


def first_nonzero_trace(g: Graph, bound: int = 12) -> Optional[int]:
    b = hashimoto(g)
    power = mat_identity(len(b))
    for n in range(1, bound + 1):
        power = mat_mul(power, b)
        if trace(power) != 0:
            return n
    return None


def reverse_walk(walk: Sequence[Dart]) -> Tuple[Dart, ...]:
    """The reversal involution: reverse the list and flip every dart."""
    return tuple((v, u) for (u, v) in reversed(list(walk)))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_main_theorem() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("1. THE TRACE FORMULA:  trace(B^n) = #rooted closed NB walks of length n")
    print("=" * 72)
    examples = [
        ("K3  (triangle)", complete_graph(3), 7),
        ("K4  (complete, 4 vertices)", complete_graph(4), 6),
        ("C5  (pentagon)", cycle_graph(5), 6),
        ("P4  (path, a tree)", path_graph(4), 6),
        ("Petersen graph", petersen_graph(), 5),
    ]
    for name, g, nmax in examples:
        print(f"\n{name}:  |V| = {g.n}, |E| = {len(g.edges)}, |darts| = {2*len(g.edges)}")
        print("   n :  trace(B^n)   enumerated   match")
        for n in range(0, nmax + 1):
            t = nb_trace(g, n)
            c = count_closed_nb_walks(g, n)
            print(f"  {n:2d} : {t:11d} {c:12d}     {'OK' if t == c else 'MISMATCH'}")
            assert t == c


def demo_small_powers() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("2. SMALL POWERS:  trace(B^0) = sum of degrees, trace(B^1) = trace(B^2) = 0,")
    print("   trace(B^3) = number of ordered triangles = 6 * #triangles")
    print("=" * 72)
    for name, g in [
        ("K3", complete_graph(3)),
        ("K4", complete_graph(4)),
        ("K5", complete_graph(5)),
        ("C5", cycle_graph(5)),
        ("Petersen", petersen_graph()),
    ]:
        degsum = sum(g.degree(v) for v in range(g.n))
        t0, t1, t2, t3 = (nb_trace(g, k) for k in range(4))
        tri = ordered_triangles(g)
        print(f"{name:9s}  trace(B^0) = {t0:3d} = sum deg = {degsum:3d} | "
              f"trace(B^1) = {t1} | trace(B^2) = {t2} | "
              f"trace(B^3) = {t3:3d} = ordered triangles = {tri:3d} "
              f"(= 6 * {tri // 6})")
        assert (t0, t1, t2, t3) == (degsum, 0, 0, tri)


def demo_parity() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("3. EVENNESS:  dart reversal is a fixed-point-free involution on the set of")
    print("   rooted closed non-backtracking walks, hence every trace is even")
    print("=" * 72)
    g = complete_graph(4)
    for n in range(1, 6):
        walks = closed_nb_walks(g, n)
        s = set(walks)
        assert all(reverse_walk(w) in s for w in walks), "reversal must preserve the set"
        assert all(reverse_walk(w) != w for w in walks), "reversal has no fixed point"
        print(f"  K4, n = {n}: {len(walks):4d} walks, "
              f"reversal is an involution without fixed points -> even: "
              f"{len(walks) % 2 == 0}")
    if walks:
        w = walks[0]
        print(f"\n  Example pairing at n = 5:\n    walk     {list(w)}\n"
              f"    reversed {list(reverse_walk(w))}")


def demo_row_sums_and_growth() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("4. ROW SUMS AND GROWTH:  row of dart (u,v) sums to deg(v) - 1;")
    print("   for a (q+1)-regular graph, trace(B^n) <= |darts| * q^n")
    print("=" * 72)
    for name, g in [("K4", complete_graph(4)), ("C5", cycle_graph(5)),
                    ("Petersen", petersen_graph())]:
        b = hashimoto(g)
        darts = g.darts()
        ok = all(sum(b[i]) == g.degree(d[1]) - 1 for i, d in enumerate(darts))
        deg = g.is_regular()
        q = None if deg is None else deg - 1
        print(f"\n{name}: row-sum identity holds for every dart: {ok}"
              + (f";  (q+1)-regular with q = {q}" if q is not None else ""))
        assert ok
        if q is not None:
            for n in range(1, 7):
                t = nb_trace(g, n)
                bound = len(darts) * q ** n
                print(f"    n = {n}: trace = {t:6d}  <=  |darts|*q^n = {bound:8d}   "
                      f"{'OK' if t <= bound else 'VIOLATED'}")
                assert t <= bound


def demo_acyclicity_and_girth() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("5. ACYCLICITY AND GIRTH:  forests have identically zero trace, and for a")
    print("   graph with a cycle, girth = min{n >= 1 : trace(B^n) != 0},")
    print("   with 2 * girth <= trace(B^girth)")
    print("=" * 72)
    forests = [
        ("path P5", path_graph(5)),
        ("star K_{1,4}", Graph(5, [(0, i) for i in range(1, 5)])),
        ("two disjoint edges", Graph(4, [(0, 1), (2, 3)])),
    ]
    for name, g in forests:
        traces = [nb_trace(g, n) for n in range(1, 9)]
        print(f"  forest {name:20s} traces n=1..8: {traces}  girth = {girth(g)}")
        assert all(t == 0 for t in traces)

    cyclic = [
        ("K3", complete_graph(3)),
        ("K4", complete_graph(4)),
        ("C5", cycle_graph(5)),
        ("C7", cycle_graph(7)),
        ("Petersen", petersen_graph()),
        ("K_{3,3}", Graph(6, [(i, 3 + j) for i in range(3) for j in range(3)])),
    ]
    print()
    for name, g in cyclic:
        gg = girth(g)
        first = first_nonzero_trace(g)
        tg = nb_trace(g, gg)
        print(f"  {name:10s} girth = {gg}, first n with trace != 0 = {first}, "
              f"trace(B^girth) = {tg:4d} >= 2*girth = {2*gg:3d}   "
              f"{'OK' if gg == first and tg >= 2*gg else 'FAIL'}")
        assert gg == first and tg >= 2 * gg
    print("\n  (For a cycle graph C_m the first nonzero trace is exactly 2m:")
    for m in (3, 4, 5, 6, 7):
        g = cycle_graph(m)
        print(f"     C{m}: trace(B^{m}) = {nb_trace(g, m)} = 2 * {m}")
        assert nb_trace(g, m) == 2 * m
    print("   the m rotations times the 2 orientations of the unique cycle.)")


def demo_monotonicity() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("6. MONOTONICITY:  if H is a subgraph of G on the same vertices, then")
    print("   trace(B_H^n) <= trace(B_G^n) for all n")
    print("=" * 72)
    chain = [
        ("C5", cycle_graph(5)),
        ("C5 + one chord", Graph(5, [(i, (i + 1) % 5) for i in range(5)] + [(0, 2)])),
        ("C5 + two chords",
         Graph(5, [(i, (i + 1) % 5) for i in range(5)] + [(0, 2), (0, 3)])),
        ("K5", complete_graph(5)),
    ]
    print("   graph              n=3    n=4    n=5    n=6")
    rows: List[List[int]] = []
    for name, g in chain:
        row = [nb_trace(g, n) for n in (3, 4, 5, 6)]
        rows.append(row)
        print(f"   {name:18s}" + "".join(f"{x:7d}" for x in row))
    for a, b in zip(rows, rows[1:]):
        assert all(x <= y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    print("   -> every column is nondecreasing, as predicted.")


def demo_triangle_periodicity() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("7. THE TRIANGLE IS A PERMUTATION:  for K3, B^3 = I, so trace(B^n) = 6 if")
    print("   3 | n and 0 otherwise; for C5, B^5 = I and trace(B^n) = 10 iff 5 | n")
    print("=" * 72)
    k3 = complete_graph(3)
    b3 = mat_pow(hashimoto(k3), 3)
    print(f"  K3: B^3 = I ?  {b3 == mat_identity(6)}")
    print("      traces n=0..9: ", [nb_trace(k3, n) for n in range(10)])
    assert b3 == mat_identity(6)
    assert [nb_trace(k3, n) for n in range(10)] == [
        6 if n % 3 == 0 else 0 for n in range(10)
    ]
    c5 = cycle_graph(5)
    b5 = mat_pow(hashimoto(c5), 5)
    print(f"  C5: B^5 = I ?  {b5 == mat_identity(10)}")
    print("      traces n=0..9: ", [nb_trace(c5, n) for n in range(10)])
    assert b5 == mat_identity(10)


def main() -> None:
    demo_main_theorem()
    demo_small_powers()
    demo_parity()
    demo_row_sums_and_growth()
    demo_acyclicity_and_girth()
    demo_monotonicity()
    demo_triangle_periodicity()
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("All demonstrations completed and all assertions passed.")
    print("=" * 72)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The Non-Backtracking Trace Formula: numerical demonstrations
============================================================

For a finite simple graph G = (V, E) let

    D = { (u, v) : {u, v} in E }

be its set of *darts* (each undirected edge gives two darts, so |D| = 2|E|).
The Hashimoto (non-backtracking) matrix B is the |D| x |D| zero-one matrix

    B[(u,v), (x,y)] = 1   iff   v = x  and  y != u.

A *rooted closed non-backtracking walk of length n* is a list of n + 1 darts
d_0, d_1, ..., d_n with B[d_i, d_{i+1}] = 1 for all i and d_0 = d_n.

Main theorem demonstrated here:

    trace(B^n) = # { rooted closed non-backtracking walks of length n }.

Together with its corollaries:

  * trace(B^0) = |D| = sum of degrees,  trace(B^1) = trace(B^2) = 0;
  * trace(B^3) = number of ordered triangles (= 6 * #triangles);
  * every trace(B^n) is even (dart reversal is a fixed-point-free involution);
  * row sums: sum_{d'} B[d, d'] = deg(head(d)) - 1; for a (q+1)-regular graph
    every row sums to q, so trace(B^n) <= |D| * q^n;
  * G is a forest  iff  trace(B^n) = 0 for all n >= 1;
  * girth(G) = min { n >= 1 : trace(B^n) != 0 }, and 2 * girth(G) <= trace(B^girth);
  * H subgraph of G  implies  trace(B_H^n) <= trace(B_G^n).

Everything below is plain Python with no third-party dependencies: the matrix
powers are computed with exact integer arithmetic, and the walk counts are
obtained by explicit enumeration, so the two sides of the theorem are compared
by two genuinely independent computations.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Vertex = int
Edge = FrozenSet[Vertex]
Dart = Tuple[Vertex, Vertex]
Matrix = List[List[int]]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Graphs
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

class Graph:
    """A finite simple graph on the vertex set {0, ..., n-1}."""

    def __init__(self, n: int, edges: Iterable[Tuple[Vertex, Vertex]]) -> None:
        self.n: int = n
        self.edges: List[Edge] = []
        seen: Set[Edge] = set()
        for u, v in edges:
            if u == v:
                raise ValueError("simple graphs have no loops")
            e = frozenset((u, v))
            if e not in seen:
                seen.add(e)
                self.edges.append(e)
        self.adj: Dict[Vertex, Set[Vertex]] = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
        for e in self.edges:
            u, v = tuple(e)
            self.adj[u].add(v)
            self.adj[v].add(u)

    def degree(self, v: Vertex) -> int:
        return len(self.adj[v])

    def darts(self) -> List[Dart]:
        """All darts, in a fixed deterministic order."""
        out: List[Dart] = []
        for e in sorted(self.edges, key=lambda s: sorted(s)):
            u, v = sorted(e)
            out.append((u, v))
            out.append((v, u))
        return out

    def is_regular(self) -> Optional[int]:
        """Return the common degree if the graph is regular, else None."""
        degs = {self.degree(v) for v in range(self.n)}
        return degs.pop() if len(degs) == 1 else None


def complete_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    return Graph(n, combinations(range(n), 2))


def cycle_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    return Graph(n, [(i, (i + 1) % n) for i in range(n)])


def path_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    return Graph(n, [(i, i + 1) for i in range(n - 1)])


def petersen_graph() -> Graph:
    outer = [(i, (i + 1) % 5) for i in range(5)]
    inner = [(5 + i, 5 + (i + 2) % 5) for i in range(5)]
    spokes = [(i, 5 + i) for i in range(5)]
    return Graph(10, outer + inner + spokes)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The Hashimoto matrix and exact integer linear algebra
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def nb_adjacent(d: Dart, e: Dart) -> bool:
    """Non-backtracking succession: d = (u,v) is followed by e = (x,y)."""
    (u, v), (x, y) = d, e
    return v == x and y != u


def hashimoto(g: Graph) -> Matrix:
    darts = g.darts()
    return [[1 if nb_adjacent(d, e) else 0 for e in darts] for d in darts]


def mat_mul(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    n, m, p = len(a), len(b), len(b[0])
    out = [[0] * p for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n):
        row = a[i]
        oi = out[i]
        for k in range(m):
            aik = row[k]
            if aik:
                bk = b[k]
                for j in range(p):
                    oi[j] += aik * bk[j]
    return out


def mat_identity(n: int) -> Matrix:
    return [[1 if i == j else 0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def mat_pow(a: Matrix, n: int) -> Matrix:
    """Exact integer matrix power by repeated squaring."""
    result = mat_identity(len(a))
    base = [row[:] for row in a]
    while n:
        if n & 1:
            result = mat_mul(result, base)
        base = mat_mul(base, base)
        n >>= 1
    return result


def trace(a: Matrix) -> int:
    return sum(a[i][i] for i in range(len(a)))


def nb_trace(g: Graph, n: int) -> int:
    return trace(mat_pow(hashimoto(g), n))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Brute-force enumeration of rooted closed non-backtracking walks
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def closed_nb_walks(g: Graph, n: int) -> List[Tuple[Dart, ...]]:
    """All rooted closed non-backtracking walks of length n, as dart lists."""
    darts = g.darts()
    if n == 0:
        return [(d,) for d in darts]
    successors: Dict[Dart, List[Dart]] = {
        d: [e for e in darts if nb_adjacent(d, e)] for d in darts
    }
    out: List[Tuple[Dart, ...]] = []

    def extend(prefix: List[Dart]) -> None:
        if len(prefix) == n + 1:
            if prefix[0] == prefix[-1]:
                out.append(tuple(prefix))
            return
        for e in successors[prefix[-1]]:
            prefix.append(e)
            extend(prefix)
            prefix.pop()

    for d in darts:
        extend([d])
    return out


def count_closed_nb_walks(g: Graph, n: int) -> int:
    return len(closed_nb_walks(g, n))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Combinatorial invariants used by the corollaries
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def ordered_triangles(g: Graph) -> int:
    """Number of triples (a,b,c) with a~b, b~c, c~a; equals 6 * #triangles."""
    return sum(
        1
        for a in range(g.n)
        for b in g.adj[a]
        for c in g.adj[b]
        if a in g.adj[c]
    )


def girth(g: Graph) -> Optional[int]:
    """Length of a shortest cycle, or None for a forest (BFS from each vertex)."""
    best: Optional[int] = None
    for root in range(g.n):
        dist = {root: 0}
        parent: Dict[Vertex, Optional[Vertex]] = {root: None}
        queue = [root]
        while queue:
            nxt: List[Vertex] = []
            for u in queue:
                for w in g.adj[u]:
                    if w not in dist:
                        dist[w] = dist[u] + 1
                        parent[w] = u
                        nxt.append(w)
                    elif parent[u] != w:
                        cand = dist[u] + dist[w] + 1
                        best = cand if best is None else min(best, cand)
            queue = nxt
    return best


def first_nonzero_trace(g: Graph, bound: int = 12) -> Optional[int]:
    b = hashimoto(g)
    power = mat_identity(len(b))
    for n in range(1, bound + 1):
        power = mat_mul(power, b)
        if trace(power) != 0:
            return n
    return None


def reverse_walk(walk: Sequence[Dart]) -> Tuple[Dart, ...]:
    """The reversal involution: reverse the list and flip every dart."""
    return tuple((v, u) for (u, v) in reversed(list(walk)))

def demo_main_theorem() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("1. THE TRACE FORMULA:  trace(B^n) = #rooted closed NB walks of length n")
    print("=" * 72)
    examples = [
        ("K3  (triangle)", complete_graph(3), 7),
        ("K4  (complete, 4 vertices)", complete_graph(4), 6),
        ("C5  (pentagon)", cycle_graph(5), 6),
        ("P4  (path, a tree)", path_graph(4), 6),
        ("Petersen graph", petersen_graph(), 5),
    ]
    for name, g, nmax in examples:
        print(f"\n{name}:  |V| = {g.n}, |E| = {len(g.edges)}, |darts| = {2*len(g.edges)}")
        print("   n :  trace(B^n)   enumerated   match")
        for n in range(0, nmax + 1):
            t = nb_trace(g, n)
            c = count_closed_nb_walks(g, n)
            print(f"  {n:2d} : {t:11d} {c:12d}     {'OK' if t == c else 'MISMATCH'}")
            assert t == c


def demo_small_powers() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("2. SMALL POWERS:  trace(B^0) = sum of degrees, trace(B^1) = trace(B^2) = 0,")
    print("   trace(B^3) = number of ordered triangles = 6 * #triangles")
    print("=" * 72)
    for name, g in [
        ("K3", complete_graph(3)),
        ("K4", complete_graph(4)),
        ("K5", complete_graph(5)),
        ("C5", cycle_graph(5)),
        ("Petersen", petersen_graph()),
    ]:
        degsum = sum(g.degree(v) for v in range(g.n))
        t0, t1, t2, t3 = (nb_trace(g, k) for k in range(4))
        tri = ordered_triangles(g)
        print(f"{name:9s}  trace(B^0) = {t0:3d} = sum deg = {degsum:3d} | "
              f"trace(B^1) = {t1} | trace(B^2) = {t2} | "
              f"trace(B^3) = {t3:3d} = ordered triangles = {tri:3d} "
              f"(= 6 * {tri // 6})")
        assert (t0, t1, t2, t3) == (degsum, 0, 0, tri)


def demo_parity() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("3. EVENNESS:  dart reversal is a fixed-point-free involution on the set of")
    print("   rooted closed non-backtracking walks, hence every trace is even")
    print("=" * 72)
    g = complete_graph(4)
    for n in range(1, 6):
        walks = closed_nb_walks(g, n)
        s = set(walks)
        assert all(reverse_walk(w) in s for w in walks), "reversal must preserve the set"
        assert all(reverse_walk(w) != w for w in walks), "reversal has no fixed point"
        print(f"  K4, n = {n}: {len(walks):4d} walks, "
              f"reversal is an involution without fixed points -> even: "
              f"{len(walks) % 2 == 0}")
    if walks:
        w = walks[0]
        print(f"\n  Example pairing at n = 5:\n    walk     {list(w)}\n"
              f"    reversed {list(reverse_walk(w))}")


def demo_row_sums_and_growth() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("4. ROW SUMS AND GROWTH:  row of dart (u,v) sums to deg(v) - 1;")
    print("   for a (q+1)-regular graph, trace(B^n) <= |darts| * q^n")
    print("=" * 72)
    for name, g in [("K4", complete_graph(4)), ("C5", cycle_graph(5)),
                    ("Petersen", petersen_graph())]:
        b = hashimoto(g)
        darts = g.darts()
        ok = all(sum(b[i]) == g.degree(d[1]) - 1 for i, d in enumerate(darts))
        deg = g.is_regular()
        q = None if deg is None else deg - 1
        print(f"\n{name}: row-sum identity holds for every dart: {ok}"
              + (f";  (q+1)-regular with q = {q}" if q is not None else ""))
        assert ok
        if q is not None:
            for n in range(1, 7):
                t = nb_trace(g, n)
                bound = len(darts) * q ** n
                print(f"    n = {n}: trace = {t:6d}  <=  |darts|*q^n = {bound:8d}   "
                      f"{'OK' if t <= bound else 'VIOLATED'}")
                assert t <= bound


def demo_acyclicity_and_girth() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("5. ACYCLICITY AND GIRTH:  forests have identically zero trace, and for a")
    print("   graph with a cycle, girth = min{n >= 1 : trace(B^n) != 0},")
    print("   with 2 * girth <= trace(B^girth)")
    print("=" * 72)
    forests = [
        ("path P5", path_graph(5)),
        ("star K_{1,4}", Graph(5, [(0, i) for i in range(1, 5)])),
        ("two disjoint edges", Graph(4, [(0, 1), (2, 3)])),
    ]
    for name, g in forests:
        traces = [nb_trace(g, n) for n in range(1, 9)]
        print(f"  forest {name:20s} traces n=1..8: {traces}  girth = {girth(g)}")
        assert all(t == 0 for t in traces)

    cyclic = [
        ("K3", complete_graph(3)),
        ("K4", complete_graph(4)),
        ("C5", cycle_graph(5)),
        ("C7", cycle_graph(7)),
        ("Petersen", petersen_graph()),
        ("K_{3,3}", Graph(6, [(i, 3 + j) for i in range(3) for j in range(3)])),
    ]
    print()
    for name, g in cyclic:
        gg = girth(g)
        first = first_nonzero_trace(g)
        tg = nb_trace(g, gg)
        print(f"  {name:10s} girth = {gg}, first n with trace != 0 = {first}, "
              f"trace(B^girth) = {tg:4d} >= 2*girth = {2*gg:3d}   "
              f"{'OK' if gg == first and tg >= 2*gg else 'FAIL'}")
        assert gg == first and tg >= 2 * gg
    print("\n  (For a cycle graph C_m the first nonzero trace is exactly 2m:")
    for m in (3, 4, 5, 6, 7):
        g = cycle_graph(m)
        print(f"     C{m}: trace(B^{m}) = {nb_trace(g, m)} = 2 * {m}")
        assert nb_trace(g, m) == 2 * m
    print("   the m rotations times the 2 orientations of the unique cycle.)")


def demo_monotonicity() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("6. MONOTONICITY:  if H is a subgraph of G on the same vertices, then")
    print("   trace(B_H^n) <= trace(B_G^n) for all n")
    print("=" * 72)
    chain = [
        ("C5", cycle_graph(5)),
        ("C5 + one chord", Graph(5, [(i, (i + 1) % 5) for i in range(5)] + [(0, 2)])),
        ("C5 + two chords",
         Graph(5, [(i, (i + 1) % 5) for i in range(5)] + [(0, 2), (0, 3)])),
        ("K5", complete_graph(5)),
    ]
    print("   graph              n=3    n=4    n=5    n=6")
    rows: List[List[int]] = []
    for name, g in chain:
        row = [nb_trace(g, n) for n in (3, 4, 5, 6)]
        rows.append(row)
        print(f"   {name:18s}" + "".join(f"{x:7d}" for x in row))
    for a, b in zip(rows, rows[1:]):
        assert all(x <= y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    print("   -> every column is nondecreasing, as predicted.")


def demo_triangle_periodicity() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("7. THE TRIANGLE IS A PERMUTATION:  for K3, B^3 = I, so trace(B^n) = 6 if")
    print("   3 | n and 0 otherwise; for C5, B^5 = I and trace(B^n) = 10 iff 5 | n")
    print("=" * 72)
    k3 = complete_graph(3)
    b3 = mat_pow(hashimoto(k3), 3)
    print(f"  K3: B^3 = I ?  {b3 == mat_identity(6)}")
    print("      traces n=0..9: ", [nb_trace(k3, n) for n in range(10)])
    assert b3 == mat_identity(6)
    assert [nb_trace(k3, n) for n in range(10)] == [
        6 if n % 3 == 0 else 0 for n in range(10)
    ]
    c5 = cycle_graph(5)
    b5 = mat_pow(hashimoto(c5), 5)
    print(f"  C5: B^5 = I ?  {b5 == mat_identity(10)}")
    print("      traces n=0..9: ", [nb_trace(c5, n) for n in range(10)])
    assert b5 == mat_identity(10)

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Dart = Tuple[int, int]
Word = Tuple[Dart, ...]


def darts_of(edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> List[Dart]:
    out: List[Dart] = []
    for u, v in sorted({(min(a, b), max(a, b)) for a, b in edges}):
        out.append((u, v))
        out.append((v, u))
    return out


def may_follow(d: Dart, e: Dart) -> bool:
    return d[1] == e[0] and e[1] != d[0]


def hashimoto(edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> List[List[int]]:
    ds = darts_of(edges)
    return [[1 if may_follow(d, e) else 0 for e in ds] for d in ds]


def mat_mul(a: List[List[int]], b: List[List[int]]) -> List[List[int]]:
    p = len(b[0])
    out = [[0] * p for _ in a]
    for i, row in enumerate(a):
        oi = out[i]
        for k, aik in enumerate(row):
            if aik:
                bk = b[k]
                for j in range(p):
                    oi[j] += aik * bk[j]
    return out


def trace_prefix(edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]], nmax: int) -> List[int]:
    b = hashimoto(edges)
    m = len(b)
    power = [[1 if i == j else 0 for j in range(m)] for i in range(m)]
    out = [m]
    for _ in range(nmax):
        power = mat_mul(power, b)
        out.append(sum(power[i][i] for i in range(m)))
    return out


def girth_bfs(n_vertices: int, edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Optional[int]:
    adj: Dict[int, Set[int]] = {v: set() for v in range(n_vertices)}
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].add(v)
        adj[v].add(u)
    best: Optional[int] = None
    for root in range(n_vertices):
        dist = {root: 0}
        par: Dict[int, Optional[int]] = {root: None}
        layer = [root]
        while layer:
            nxt: List[int] = []
            for u in layer:
                for w in adj[u]:
                    if w not in dist:
                        dist[w] = dist[u] + 1
                        par[w] = u
                        nxt.append(w)
                    elif par[u] != w:
                        cand = dist[u] + dist[w] + 1
                        best = cand if best is None else min(best, cand)
            layer = nxt
    return best


def cyclic_nb_words(edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]], n: int) -> List[Word]:
    ds = darts_of(edges)
    succ: Dict[Dart, List[Dart]] = {d: [e for e in ds if may_follow(d, e)] for d in ds}
    out: List[Word] = []

    def extend(word: List[Dart]) -> None:
        if len(word) == n:
            if may_follow(word[-1], word[0]):
                out.append(tuple(word))
            return
        for e in succ[word[-1]]:
            word.append(e)
            extend(word)
            word.pop()

    for d in ds:
        extend([d])
    return out


def dihedral_orbits(words: Sequence[Word]) -> List[List[Word]]:
    pool: Set[Word] = set(words)
    orbits: List[List[Word]] = []
    while pool:
        w = next(iter(pool))
        n = len(w)
        rev = tuple((v, u) for (u, v) in reversed(w))
        orb = {w[i:] + w[:i] for i in range(n)} | {rev[i:] + rev[:i] for i in range(n)}
        orb &= pool
        pool -= orb
        orbits.append(sorted(orb))
    return orbits


GRAPHS: List[Tuple[str, int, List[Tuple[int, int]]]] = [
    ("path P5 (tree)", 5, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)]),
    ("star K1,4 (tree)", 5, [(0, i) for i in range(1, 5)]),
    ("K3", 3, list(combinations(range(3), 2))),
    ("K4", 4, list(combinations(range(4), 2))),
    ("K5", 5, list(combinations(range(5), 2))),
    ("C5", 5, [(i, (i + 1) % 5) for i in range(5)]),
    ("C7", 7, [(i, (i + 1) % 7) for i in range(7)]),
    ("K3,3", 6, [(i, 3 + j) for i in range(3) for j in range(3)]),
    ("cube Q3", 8, [(u, u ^ (1 << b)) for u in range(8) for b in range(3)
                    if u < (u ^ (1 << b))]),
    ("Petersen", 10,
     [(i, (i + 1) % 5) for i in range(5)]
     + [(5 + i, 5 + (i + 2) % 5) for i in range(5)]
     + [(i, 5 + i) for i in range(5)]),
]


def main() -> None:
    print(f"{'graph':18s}{'girth(BFS)':>11s}{'first n':>9s}{'trace':>8s}"
          f"{'orbits':>8s}{'2g*orbits':>11s}  verdict")
    print("-" * 78)
    for name, nv, edges in GRAPHS:
        g_bfs = girth_bfs(nv, edges)
        seq = trace_prefix(edges, min(nv, 8))
        first = next((n for n in range(1, len(seq)) if seq[n] != 0), None)
        if g_bfs is None:
            assert all(t == 0 for t in seq[1:])
            print(f"{name:18s}{'inf':>11s}{'none':>9s}{'0':>8s}{'-':>8s}{'-':>11s}"
                  f"  forest: the whole sequence vanishes")
            continue
        assert first == g_bfs, (name, first, g_bfs)
        words = cyclic_nb_words(edges, g_bfs)
        orbits = dihedral_orbits(words)
        pred = 2 * g_bfs * len(orbits)
        full = all(len(o) == 2 * g_bfs for o in orbits)

Dart = Tuple[int, int]

def darts_of(edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> List[Dart]:

    ds = darts_of(edges)

    out: List[Walk] = []

        if len(path) == n + 1:

            return

            path.append(e)
            extend(path)
            path.pop()

def darts(n_vertices: int, edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> List[Dart]:

    b = [[1 if may_follow(d, e) else 0 for e in ds] for d in ds]

Dart = Tuple[int, int]


def _darts(edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> List[Dart]:
    out: List[Dart] = []

        out.append((v, u))

def _successors(ds: Sequence[Dart]) -> List[List[int]]:
    index: Dict[Dart, int] = {d: i for i, d in enumerate(ds)}
    out_of: Dict[int, List[Dart]] = {}

def trace_sequence(n_vertices: int,
                   edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]],
                   nmax: int) -> List[int]:
    """[trace(B^0), ..., trace(B^nmax)], computed with sparse matrix-vector products.

    trace(B^n) = sum over darts d of (B^n)[d, d]; the d-th diagonal entry is obtained by
    propagating the indicator vector of d forward n steps along successor lists.

    ds = _darts(edges)
    succ = _successors(ds)
    m = len(ds)
    out = [m]
    for n in range(1, nmax + 1):

        for start in range(m):

            vec[start] = 1
            for _ in range(n):
                nxt = [0] * m
                for i, x in enumerate(vec):
                    if x:
                        for j in succ[i]:

            total += vec[start]

    walk of length n forces a cycle of length at most n.  A graph with a cycle has girth
    at most |V|, which bounds the search.

    seq = trace_sequence(n_vertices, edges, max(n_vertices, 1))
    for n in range(1, len(seq)):
        if seq[n] != 0:

    return None


def count_closed_nb_walks(n_vertices: int,
                          edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]],
                          n: int) -> int:
    """Brute-force count of rooted closed non-backtracking walks of length n."""
    ds = _darts(edges)
    if n == 0:
        return len(ds)
    succ = _successors(ds)
    total = 0

    def extend(start: int, cur: int, steps: int) -> None:
        nonlocal total
        if steps == n:
            if cur == start:
                total += 1
            return
        for j in succ[cur]:
            extend(start, j, steps + 1)

    for s in range(len(ds)):
        extend(s, s, 0)
    return total

        if len(word) == n:
            if may_follow(word[-1], word[0]):

            return

            word.append(e)
            extend(word)
            word.pop()

def mat_mul(a: List[List[int]], b: List[List[int]]) -> List[List[int]]:
    p = len(b[0])
    out = [[0] * p for _ in a]
    for i, row in enumerate(a):
        oi = out[i]
        for k, aik in enumerate(row):
            if aik:
                bk = b[k]
                for j in range(p):
                    oi[j] += aik * bk[j]
    return out


def trace_sequence(n: int, edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]], nmax: int) -> List[int]:
    b = hashimoto(n, edges)
    size = len(b)
    power = [[1 if i == j else 0 for j in range(size)] for i in range(size)]
    out = [size]
    for _ in range(nmax):
        power = mat_mul(power, b)
        out.append(sum(power[i][i] for i in range(size)))
    return out


def girth_bfs(n: int, edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Optional[int]:
    adj: Dict[int, Set[int]] = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].add(v)
        adj[v].add(u)
    best: Optional[int] = None
    for root in range(n):
        dist = {root: 0}
        par: Dict[int, Optional[int]] = {root: None}
        layer = [root]
        while layer:
            nxt: List[int] = []
            for u in layer:
                for w in adj[u]:

                        dist[w] = dist[u] + 1
                        par[w] = u
                        nxt.append(w)
                    elif par[u] != w:
                        cand = dist[u] + dist[w] + 1
                        best = cand if best is None else min(best, cand)

    return best

For a (q+1)-regular graph the eigenvalues of the non-backtracking matrix B split into a

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

Dart = Tuple[int, int]


def darts_of(edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> List[Dart]:
    out: List[Dart] = []
    for u, v in edges:
        out.append((u, v))
        out.append((v, u))
    return out


def hashimoto(edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> np.ndarray:
    ds = darts_of(edges)
    m = len(ds)
    b = np.zeros((m, m))
    for i, (u, v) in enumerate(ds):
        for j, (x, y) in enumerate(ds):
            if v == x and y != u:
                b[i, j] = 1.0
    return b


def petersen() -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    return ([(i, (i + 1) % 5) for i in range(5)]
            + [(5 + i, 5 + (i + 2) % 5) for i in range(5)]
            + [(i, 5 + i) for i in range(5)])


def cube_graph() -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """The 3-cube Q3: vertices are 0..7, adjacent when they differ in one bit."""
    return [(u, u ^ (1 << b)) for u in range(8) for b in range(3) if u < (u ^ (1 << b))]


GRAPHS: List[Tuple[str, int, List[Tuple[int, int]]]] = [
    ("K₄  (q = 2)", 2, list(combinations(range(4), 2))),
    ("Q₃, the cube  (q = 2)", 2, cube_graph()),
    ("Petersen  (q = 2)", 2, petersen()),
    ("K₆  (q = 4)", 4, list(combinations(range(6), 2))),
]


def main() -> None:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 4.3))
    for ax, (name, q, edges) in zip(axes, GRAPHS):
        b = hashimoto(edges)
        ev = np.linalg.eigvals(b)
        theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 400)
        ax.plot(np.sqrt(q) * np.cos(theta), np.sqrt(q) * np.sin(theta),
                color="#ff9f43", lw=1.6, label=r"$|z|=\sqrt{q}$")
        ax.plot(q * np.cos(theta), q * np.sin(theta),
                color="#576574", lw=1.0, ls="--", label=r"$|z|=q$")
        ax.scatter(ev.real, ev.imag, s=26, color="#0abde3",
                   edgecolor="#0c2461", linewidth=0.4, zorder=3)
        ax.axhline(0, color="#dfe4ea", lw=0.6)
        ax.axvline(0, color="#dfe4ea", lw=0.6)
        ax.set_aspect("equal")
        ax.set_title(f"{name}\n{b.shape[0]} darts", fontsize=10)
        ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
        lim = q + 0.6
        ax.set_xlim(-lim, lim)
        ax.set_ylim(-lim, lim)
        ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower left", frameon=False)

    fig.suptitle("Spectra of the non-backtracking matrix: the bulk sits on the circle of "
                 r"radius $\sqrt{q}$, the Perron eigenvalue at $q$", fontsize=12)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("nb_spectrum.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote nb_spectrum.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
